title: The kings who couldn't lose
hook: kings who couldn't lift it decided to take Mithila instead
carry: ahamkara: the ego that can't bear to fail

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughter of the furrow: Shiva's bow from Daksha's rite, and Sita, found in the earth. Your line was bhumi devi, the earth is a mother.
screen: `BHUMI DEVI: THE EARTH IS A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Janaka made a decision about his daughter, and he announced it. Sita, he said, is viryashulka: the price of her hand is strength. Not gold, not alliances, not land. Whoever can lift and string Shiva's bow may marry her. Word spread. Kings came from everywhere to try, and every one of them failed. Then, Janaka tells Vishvamitra, something ugly happened. Wounded pride doesn't always go home quietly. Sometimes it comes back with an army.
screen: `THE PRICE OF HER HAND: STRENGTH.` → `KINGS COME FROM EVERYWHERE.` → `EVERY ONE OF THEM FAILS.`

segments.voice: The kings who failed were furious, insulted by a bow. They joined forces and laid siege to Mithila, and for a whole year the city was surrounded and supplies ran low. Janaka couldn't match their armies. So he turned to austerity and prayer, and the gods answered him with an army of their own. The kings were scattered and fled. Hindu teaching has a name for what drove those kings: ahamkara. Literally, the I-maker. It's the part of us that says: this is about me, my name, my standing. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces how a mind fixed on itself goes wrong, one step at a time. Dwelling on something breeds clinging, clinging breeds wanting, wanting breeds anger, and anger clouds the mind. That's the siege, step by step. The kings didn't really lose a bride; they lost face, and ahamkara can't bear that. Now look at Janaka. No army, no way to win, and still he keeps his word: strength earns his daughter, not force. He sets down his own pride and turns to the gods. That's the spirit behind a small ritual you'll see at temples. Many Hindus break a coconut before God, and families often explain it this way: the hard shell is the ego, cracked open so what's sweet inside can be offered. So when Janaka finally shows Rama the bow, it's no party trick. It arrives in an iron chest on an eight-wheeled cart, hauled in, the text says, by five thousand strong men. The whole hall waits to see what the young prince will do.
screen: `THE KINGS FAIL, AND BESIEGE MITHILA.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `CLINGING, WANTING, ANGER.` · `JANAKA KEEPS HIS WORD.` · `THE COCONUT: A SHELL CRACKED OPEN.` · then, large: `THE HALL WAITS.`

segments.voice: Remember a time something didn't go your way in front of others, and feel where the sting lands. That's ahamkara, the I-maker. Don't fight it. On each breath out, picture it as a hard shell cracking a little, like a coconut offered at a temple. If you pray, offer the sting to God. If you don't, let the memory sit there, smaller.
Janaka's bow. The bow no king could lift, set as the price of Sita's hand. Failing to lift it sent proud kings to besiege Mithila for a year.
Your line: ahamkara, the ego that can't bear to fail. The kings had armies; Janaka had his word. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Across India, the contest of the bow is staged in Ramlila performances; later retellings such as the Ramcharitmanas present it as a swayamvara, while Valmiki describes Sita as viryashulka, won by strength.

original.note: Sanskrit ahaṃkāra: aham, I, plus kāra, maker. the sense of 'me' that takes everything personally.

trapdoor: what you thought: suitors came, failed, and that was that.
what it means: wounded ahamkara turned a contest into a year-long siege; Janaka, with no army, kept his word and prayed.
what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 66–67 call Sita viryashulka; the siege lasts a year and ends when the gods grant Janaka a fourfold army; the bow arrives in an iron casket on an eight-wheeled cart.

chat.meaning: Many Hindus explain breaking a coconut as cracking ahamkara, the ego, to offer what's inside. The kings at Mithila never let theirs crack.
